The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.\n\nFor the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}p(\\lambda ) & =\\text{det}(A-\\lambda I) \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}1-\\lambda  & 2 \\\\ 3 & 4-\\lambda \\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(1-\\lambda )(4-\\lambda )-6 \\\\  & ={\\lambda }^{2}-5\\lambda -2,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nso the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that\n\n$$\np(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.\n$$\n\nNow, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\\\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\\\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen we have\n\n$$\nf(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,\n$$\n\nand because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\\cdot 0+A+2I \\\\  & =0+A+2I \\\\  & =A+2I.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the computation is much faster:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 4\\end{aligned}]+2[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 6\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result\n\n$$\nf(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)\n$$\n\nwhere $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial\n\n$$\nf(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2\n$$\n\nfor the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!\n\nLuckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.\n\nFor the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}p(\\lambda ) & =\\text{det}(A-\\lambda I) \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}1-\\lambda  & 2 \\\\ 3 & 4-\\lambda \\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(1-\\lambda )(4-\\lambda )-6 \\\\  & ={\\lambda }^{2}-5\\lambda -2,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nso the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that\n\n$$\np(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.\n$$\n\nNow, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\\\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\\\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen we have\n\n$$\nf(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,\n$$\n\nand because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\\cdot 0+A+2I \\\\  & =0+A+2I \\\\  & =A+2I.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, the computation is much faster:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 4\\end{aligned}]+2[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 6\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result\n\n$$\nf(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)\n$$\n\nwhere $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder.
